title: IBEW Local 701 (DuPage) — Practice Exam, Form A

passages.title: Why Water Towers Stand So Tall
passages.text:
A municipal water tower is not a storage tank that happens to sit on legs. Its
height is the entire point. Water pressure in a distribution system comes from
elevation, and every foot of height adds roughly 0.43 pounds per square inch at
the ground below. A tank standing 150 feet above the neighborhood it serves
therefore delivers about 65 pounds per square inch at street level, which is
close to the range most household fixtures are designed to accept.

This arrangement lets a utility size its pumps for average demand rather than
peak demand. Pumps run steadily through the night, when electricity is cheaper
and consumption is low, filling the tank. During the morning rush, when
thousands of households draw water at once, the tank empties faster than the
pumps refill it, and gravity covers the difference. Without the tower, the
utility would need pumps large enough to meet the highest demand of the year,
and those pumps would sit idle most of the time.

The stored volume matters for a second reason that has nothing to do with daily
demand. Fire flow can require several thousand gallons per minute for hours at a
stretch, far beyond what distribution pumps supply. A full tower is a reserve
that begins delivering the instant a hydrant opens, with no startup delay and no
dependence on the electrical grid. During a power failure, a water tower keeps
supplying pressure until it drains, which is why many utilities treat tank level
as a measure of how long they can operate blind.

The shape of the tank follows from these demands. Engineers prefer a design in
which most of the stored water sits near the top, because pressure at the ground
depends on the height of the water surface, not on the total volume held. A tank
that drains from a tall, narrow column would see its pressure fall steadily as
the level dropped. A tank with a wide bowl high on a single pedestal keeps the
water surface within a narrow band of elevation through most of its useful
range, so pressure at the customer's tap stays nearly constant as the tank
empties.

passages.title: Keeping the Grid at Sixty Cycles
passages.text:
An alternating-current power grid has a heartbeat, and in North America that
heartbeat is sixty cycles per second. The figure is not a target the operators
aim at so much as a reading they watch. Frequency on a grid is a direct
consequence of the balance between how much power generators are producing and
how much load is drawing. When generation exceeds demand, the spinning machines
speed up and frequency rises. When demand exceeds generation, the machines are
dragged down and frequency falls. Nobody sets the number; the physics reports
it.

That relationship makes frequency the most convenient signal in the whole
system. A control room thousands of miles from a failed generator learns of the
failure almost instantly, because the deviation appears everywhere at once on an
interconnected grid. Operators do not need to know which machine tripped in
order to begin responding. They need only see that the balance has moved, and in
which direction.

The response happens in layers, distinguished by how quickly each acts. The
first layer is not a decision at all but inertia: the rotating mass of every
turbine and generator still connected resists any change in speed, and in doing
so donates kinetic energy to the grid during the first seconds of a shortfall.
This buys time and nothing else, but the time is essential. The second layer,
governor response, arrives within seconds as individual units sense the
frequency drop and open their valves slightly. The third, automatic generation
control, works over minutes to return frequency exactly to sixty and to restore
the reserves that the first two layers spent.

The growth of generation that connects through power electronics rather than
through a spinning shaft has complicated the first layer in particular. Solar
arrays and battery installations have no rotating mass to contribute, so a grid
with a large share of such resources has less natural inertia and its frequency
falls faster after a loss. Engineers have responded by programming inverters to
imitate the behavior they displaced, detecting a frequency change and injecting
power within milliseconds. The imitation is deliberate, and in some respects it
outperforms the original, since a programmed response can be tuned while the
physics of a spinning mass cannot.

passages.title: The Box That Rearranged the World
passages.text:
Before the shipping container, loading a cargo ship was a craft. Longshoremen
moved barrels, sacks and crates one lot at a time, fitting irregular goods into
an irregular hold in an order that had to be worked out on the spot. A ship
might spend as long in port as it spent at sea. Cargo handling, not the voyage,
was the expensive part of shipping, and it was expensive chiefly because it
consumed labor and time in roughly equal measure.

The container did not solve this problem by being a better box. Boxes were not
the difficulty. What the container did was standardize the unit of cargo so that
every step of the journey could be mechanized around the same dimensions. A
crane that could lift one container could lift them all. A chassis that fit one
would fit any. The gain came not from the steel but from the agreement, and the
agreement took longer to reach than the engineering did.

The consequences reached well beyond the docks. When moving goods became cheap
and predictable, the calculation that had tied factories to their customers
loosened. A manufacturer could put a plant where labor or materials were
advantageous rather than where the market happened to be, because the cost of
bridging the distance had fallen to a rounding error in the price of the
finished product. Whole industries relocated over the following decades, and
economists still argue about how much of that shift to attribute to the
container and how much to trade policy that arrived alongside it.

The costs fell unevenly, as such changes usually do. Ports that could not
accommodate the cranes and the land area the new system demanded declined
quickly, sometimes within a decade, while ports with deep water and room to
expand grew into the hubs the system required. The workforce contracted sharply.
A job that had rewarded experience in stowing an awkward hold became a job
operating a machine to a fixed procedure. Historians of the period generally
treat the container as a case in which a change framed as a simple efficiency
turned out to redistribute work and wealth on a scale nobody had forecast.

passages.title: Room to Move
passages.text:
Nearly every solid expands when heated, and the amount is small enough to ignore
in casual life and far too large to ignore in construction. A steel beam a
hundred feet long grows roughly three quarters of an inch over a temperature
swing of a hundred degrees Fahrenheit. That figure sounds modest until one
considers what happens if the beam is not permitted to grow. The expansion does
not simply fail to occur. The material develops internal stress instead, and the
stress a restrained member generates is set by the stiffness of the material
rather than by the size of the movement prevented. For steel the resulting
forces are large enough to buckle a member or to crack whatever is holding it.

Designers therefore spend a surprising amount of effort providing somewhere for
movement to go. A bridge deck rides on bearings that permit it to slide, and the
familiar toothed joint at each end exists to let the deck lengthen without
pressing against the abutment. Long runs of pipe are routed with deliberate
bends, or fitted with loops, so that thermal growth is absorbed by flexing
rather than by thrust against the anchors. Masonry walls receive soft joints at
intervals for the same reason. In each case the design accepts the movement as
inevitable and directs it, rather than attempting to prevent it.

Trouble arises most often where two materials meet. Aluminum expands about twice
as much as steel for the same temperature change, and concrete falls between
them. A joint that fastens dissimilar materials rigidly will work itself loose
over many cycles, or will concentrate stress at the fastener until something
yields, even though neither material alone would have been overstressed. The
failure belongs to the connection rather than to either component.

The same principle appears wherever temperature varies and materials differ, and
the remedy is nearly always the same. Slotted holes, flexible connectors and
deliberate gaps are not concessions to sloppy work. They are the acknowledgment
that a structure exposed to weather is never quite the same size twice, and that
a design which assumes otherwise will find its own way to relieve the stress.

questions.stem: If 7x − 4 = 31, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Undo the subtraction first: 7x = 31 + 4 = 35. Then divide both sides by 7, giving x = 5.
distractorNotes: subtracted 4 instead of adding it when undoing −4
added 4 to 31 but then divided by the wrong number
divided by 7 without first undoing the −4

questions.stem: If (2/3)x + 5 = 13, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Subtract 5 from both sides to get (2/3)x = 8, then multiply both sides by the reciprocal 3/2. That gives x = 12.
distractorNotes: multiplied by 2/3 instead of by its reciprocal
divided before subtracting the 5
stopped after subtracting 5 and never undid the 2/3

questions.stem: Solve for x:  3(2x − 5) = 4x + 7
questions.explanation: Distributing gives 6x − 15 = 4x + 7. Subtract 4x and add 15 to both sides: 2x = 22, so x = 11.
distractorNotes: distributed the 3 to 2x but not to −5
subtracted 15 from 7 instead of adding it to both sides
added the x-terms instead of subtracting 4x from both sides

questions.stem: The formula P = 2L + 2W gives the perimeter of a rectangle. Which expression gives W in terms of P and L?
choices: W = P − 2L
questions.explanation: Subtract 2L from both sides to get P − 2L = 2W, then divide both sides by 2. Note that dividing P − 2L by 2 leaves L, not L/2.
distractorNotes: subtracted 2L but never divided by 2
added 2L instead of subtracting it
divided the L term by 2 a second time

questions.stem: If y = 2x + 1 and 3x + y = 16, what is the value of y?
questions.explanation: Substitute 2x + 1 for y: 3x + (2x + 1) = 16, so 5x = 15 and x = 3. Then y = 2(3) + 1 = 7.
distractorNotes: solved for x and stopped without finding y
dropped the +1 when substituting into the second equation
added 1 to 16 instead of subtracting it

questions.stem: Solve the system:  4x + 3y = 27  and  2x − 3y = 3.  What is x + y?
questions.explanation: Adding the two equations eliminates y: 6x = 30, so x = 5. Substituting back gives 3y = 7, y = 7/3. Their sum is 5 + 7/3 = 22/3.
distractorNotes: found x and reported it instead of x + y
subtracted the two values instead of adding them
subtracted the constants when adding the equations

questions.stem: Simplify:  (3x³)(4x⁵)
choices: 12x²
12x¹⁵
7x⁸
12x⁸
questions.explanation: Multiply the coefficients and add the exponents: 3 × 4 = 12 and x³ · x⁵ = x⁸.
distractorNotes: subtracted the exponents instead of adding them
multiplied the exponents instead of adding them
added the coefficients instead of multiplying them

questions.stem: Simplify:  (2x⁴)³
choices: 8x¹²
2x¹²
6x¹²
8x⁷
questions.explanation: Every factor inside the parentheses is cubed: 2³ = 8, and x⁴ raised to the third power multiplies the exponents to give x¹².
distractorNotes: raised x to the third power but left the 2 alone
multiplied the base 2 by 3 instead of cubing it
added the exponents instead of multiplying them

questions.stem: What is the value of 2⁻⁴?
questions.explanation: A negative exponent means the reciprocal of the positive power: 2⁻⁴ = 1/2⁴ = 1/16. The result is positive.
distractorNotes: kept a negative sign that the reciprocal does not produce
treated the negative exponent as a negative result
used 2³ instead of 2⁴ in the denominator

questions.stem: Multiply:  (x + 6)(x − 4)
choices: x² − 24
questions.explanation: The outer and inner products are −4x and +6x, which combine to +2x, and the last terms give 6 × (−4) = −24.
distractorNotes: subtracted the outer and inner terms instead of adding −4x and 6x
added 6 and 4 instead of combining +6x and −4x
multiplied the first and last terms only and dropped the middle terms

questions.stem: Factor completely:  x² − 7x + 12
questions.explanation: Two numbers that multiply to +12 and add to −7 are −3 and −4, so the quadratic factors into those two binomials.
distractorNotes: ignored that a positive constant with a negative middle term needs two negative factors
picked factors of 12 that add to 8, not 7
picked factors of 12 that add to 13, not 7

questions.stem: Factor:  9x² − 25
questions.explanation: This is a difference of two squares: the square root of 9x² is 3x and the square root of 25 is 5, giving a sum factor and a difference factor.
distractorNotes: used 9 as the square root of 9x² instead of 3x
used the same sign twice instead of opposite signs
used 25 instead of its square root 5

questions.stem: If f(x) = 3x² − 2x + 1, what is f(−2)?
questions.explanation: Squaring −2 gives +4, so the first term is 12. The middle term is −2(−2) = +4. Adding the constant gives 12 + 4 + 1 = 17.
distractorNotes: substituted +2 instead of −2
squared before applying the negative, making the first term negative
dropped the constant term when adding up

questions.stem: If f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x², what is f(g(3))?
questions.explanation: Work from the inside out: g(3) = 9, then f(9) = 2(9) + 3 = 21.
distractorNotes: applied the functions in the reverse order
multiplied the two results instead of substituting one into the other
stopped at the inner function and never applied the outer one

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line through the points (2, −3) and (6, 5)?
questions.explanation: Slope is the change in y over the change in x: (5 − (−3)) divided by (6 − 2) = 8/4 = 2.
distractorNotes: added the x-values in the denominator instead of subtracting them
divided the run by the rise instead of the rise by the run
subtracted the y-values in one order and the x-values in the other

questions.stem: A line is given by y = −3x + 7. What is y when x = 4?
questions.explanation: Substitute 4 for x: −3(4) = −12, then add the intercept 7 to get −5.
distractorNotes: ignored the negative sign on the slope
added 7 to x before multiplying instead of after
subtracted the intercept instead of adding it

questions.stem: Solve for x:  −4x + 9 > 25
questions.explanation: Subtract 9 to get −4x > 16. Dividing both sides by −4 reverses the inequality, giving x less than −4.
distractorNotes: divided 16 by −4 but kept the result positive
did not reverse the inequality sign when dividing by a negative
both dropped the sign reversal and lost the negative

questions.stem: Solve:  −1 ≤ 2x − 5 ≤ 7
questions.explanation: Add 5 to all three parts to get 4 ≤ 2x ≤ 12, then divide all three parts by 2.
distractorNotes: subtracted 5 from the outer parts instead of adding it
added 5 correctly but never divided by 2
divided only the left-hand part by 2

questions.stem: If 3/8 = x/56, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Cross-multiply: 8x = 3 × 56 = 168, so x = 21.
distractorNotes: treated the proportion as a difference instead of a ratio
cross-multiplied in the wrong direction
divided 56 by 8 and forgot to multiply by 3

questions.stem: A crew's hourly output rises from 40 units to 46 units. What is the percent increase?
questions.explanation: Percent increase divides the change by the original amount: 6/40 = 0.15, which is 15%.
distractorNotes: divided the change by the new value instead of the original
found the new value as a percent of the old instead of the increase
reported the raw change as if it were a percent

questions.stem: y varies directly with x. When x = 4, y = 18. What is y when x = 10?
questions.explanation: Direct variation means y/x is constant: 18/4 = 4.5. Multiplying by x = 10 gives y = 45.
distractorNotes: added the constant of variation to x instead of multiplying
set up the proportion inversely instead of directly
added the change in x to y instead of scaling y

questions.stem: y varies inversely with x. When x = 5, y = 12. What is y when x = 15?
questions.explanation: Inverse variation means the product xy is constant: 5 × 12 = 60. Dividing 60 by the new x = 15 gives y = 4.
distractorNotes: used direct variation instead of inverse
subtracted the change in x from y
inverted the wrong pair of values

questions.stem: What is the larger solution of x² + 2x − 15 = 0?
questions.explanation: The quadratic factors using two numbers that multiply to −15 and add to +2, namely +5 and −3. The solutions are −5 and 3, and the larger is 3.
distractorNotes: identified both roots but reported the smaller one
reversed the signs of the factors
read the constant term as a solution

questions.stem: Simplify:  (x² − 9) / (x + 3),  where x ≠ −3
choices: x² − 3
questions.explanation: Factor the numerator as a difference of squares into (x + 3)(x − 3). The (x + 3) cancels with the denominator, leaving x − 3.
distractorNotes: cancelled to the wrong one of the two factors
cancelled the 3 from the numerator's constant only
cancelled the x terms rather than factoring first

questions.stem: Simplify:  √72
questions.explanation: 72 factors as 36 × 2, and the square root of 36 is 6, so a 6 comes out and the 2 stays under the radical.
distractorNotes: used 64 × 3, which is not 72
swapped the factor taken out with the one left under the radical
took 36 out of the radical without taking its square root

questions.stem: If |2x − 3| = 11, what is the sum of all possible values of x?
questions.explanation: The expression inside equals either 11 or −11, giving x = 7 and x = −4. Their sum is 3.
distractorNotes: found only the negative case and ignored the positive one
found only the positive case and ignored the negative one
subtracted the two solutions instead of adding them

questions.stem: What number comes next in the series?   4, 9, 14, 19, __
questions.explanation: Each term is 5 more than the one before it, so the next term is 19 + 5 = 24.
distractorNotes: used the first term as the common difference
doubled the last term instead of adding the difference
misread the difference as 6

questions.stem: What number comes next in the series?   3, 6, 12, 24, __
questions.explanation: Each term is twice the one before it, so the next term is 24 × 2 = 48.
distractorNotes: used the first term as a common difference
added the last difference instead of doubling
tripled instead of doubled

questions.stem: What number comes next in the series?   2, 5, 4, 7, 6, __
questions.explanation: The series alternates between adding 3 and subtracting 1. The last step was a subtraction, so the next step adds 3 to give 9.
distractorNotes: read the pattern as a simple alternating increase of 1
continued with the subtract-1 step instead of the add-3 step
averaged the two steps instead of alternating them

questions.stem: A tank holds 12 gallons of a 30% antifreeze mixture. How many gallons of a 60% mixture must be added to bring the tank to a 40% mixture?
questions.explanation: The antifreeze already present is 3.6 gallons. Adding x gallons at 60% must satisfy 3.6 + 0.6x = 0.4(12 + x), which simplifies to 0.2x = 1.2, so 6 gallons are needed.
distractorNotes: applied the 40% target only to the original 12 gallons, ignoring that the added gallons raise the total volume too
assumed equal parts of the two mixtures
solved for the total volume rather than the amount added

questions.stem: One worker can complete a task in 6 hours and another can complete the same task in 3 hours. Working together at these rates, how many hours does the task take?
questions.explanation: Their rates add: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 of the task per hour. The time is the reciprocal of that rate, so 2 hours.
distractorNotes: averaged the two times instead of adding the rates
subtracted the times
added the rates but did not invert the result

questions.stem: A truck leaves at 7:00 a.m. and travels 165 miles at an average speed of 55 miles per hour. At what time does it arrive?
questions.explanation: Dividing 165 miles by 55 miles per hour gives exactly 3 hours, and 3 hours after 7:00 a.m. is 10:00 a.m.
distractorNotes: divided by 55 but subtracted an hour when adding to the start time
used 4 hours, which corresponds to 220 miles, not 165
carried a half hour that the exact division does not produce

questions.stem: Multiply and express the result in scientific notation:  (3.0 × 10⁴)(2.0 × 10⁻⁶)
questions.explanation: Multiply the mantissas to get 6.0 and add the exponents: 4 + (−6) = −2.
distractorNotes: added the mantissas instead of multiplying them
multiplied the exponents instead of adding them
subtracted the exponents in the wrong order

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Water towers are an outdated technology that modern pumps have largely replaced.
A water tower's height and shape both follow from the need for steady pressure and reserve.
Municipal utilities use water towers mainly to reduce their nighttime electricity costs.
The chief purpose of a water tower is to guarantee water during a fire.
questions.explanation: The passage moves through pressure from elevation, pump sizing, fire reserve and finally tank shape, and each of those is tied back to delivering steady pressure and holding a reserve.
distractorNotes: contradicts the passage, which presents towers as actively useful
takes one supporting detail and treats it as the whole point
names one of several purposes as though it were the only one

questions.stem: According to the passage, about how much pressure does each foot of height add?
choices: About 1.5 pounds per square inch
About 0.65 pounds per square inch
About 0.43 pounds per square inch
About 4.3 pounds per square inch
questions.explanation: The passage states directly that every foot of height adds roughly 0.43 pounds per square inch.
distractorNotes: derives from the 150-foot height rather than the stated rate
borrows a digit from the 65 psi figure, which is a total, not a per-foot rate
misplaces the decimal point in the stated rate

questions.stem: The passage suggests that without a water tower, a utility would most likely have to
choices: buy larger pumps that would run below capacity much of the time
raise the price of water to cover the higher nighttime electricity costs it would face
reduce the pressure available at household fixtures
build a second tower at a different elevation
questions.explanation: The passage says the tower lets a utility size pumps for average rather than peak demand, and that without it the pumps would have to meet the year's highest demand and would sit idle most of the time.
distractorNotes: reverses the passage, which says nighttime electricity is the cheaper period
assumes a consequence the passage never draws
offers an outside solution the passage does not mention

questions.stem: As used in the final paragraph, the phrase "useful range" most nearly means
choices: the maximum volume the tank was designed to hold
the distance the water can travel through the distribution system
the variety of purposes the tower can serve
the span of tank levels over which the tower still does its job
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts water surface elevation with total volume and describes pressure staying nearly constant as the tank empties, so the phrase refers to the span of levels over which the tower still performs.
distractorNotes: substitutes total volume, which the paragraph explicitly sets aside
reads 'range' as horizontal distance rather than a span of levels
reads 'range' as variety, which the sentence's focus on level does not support

questions.stem: The passage says fire flow can demand
choices: more water than the tower itself can hold
several hundred gallons per minute for hours
several thousand gallons per hour for minutes
several thousand gallons per minute for hours
questions.explanation: The passage gives fire flow as several thousand gallons per minute for hours at a stretch.
distractorNotes: states a comparison the passage does not make
understates the figure given
swaps the units of rate and duration

questions.stem: The author mentions power failures chiefly in order to
choices: argue that utilities should invest in backup generators
warn that water service is fragile during storms
show that the tower supplies pressure without the electrical grid
explain why pumps are sized for average demand
questions.explanation: The power-failure sentence follows the claim that a full tower delivers with no startup delay and no dependence on the grid, and it illustrates that independence.
distractorNotes: recommends an action the passage never proposes
adopts an alarmed tone the passage does not take
attaches the example to the wrong argument in the passage

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a tall narrow tank would be a poor design mainly because
choices: it would hold far too little water to be of any use during a fire
its pressure would drop noticeably as the water level fell
it would cost more to build than a bowl on a pedestal
it would freeze more readily in cold weather
questions.explanation: The passage says pressure depends on the height of the water surface, and that a tank draining from a tall narrow column would see pressure fall steadily as the level dropped.
distractorNotes: raises a volume objection the passage does not make about this shape
introduces cost, which the passage never discusses
brings in an outside concern absent from the passage

questions.stem: Which best describes how the passage is organized?
choices: A common belief is introduced and then refuted with evidence
A principle is stated, then its consequences are developed in turn
Two competing designs are compared point by point throughout
A chronological account traces the development of a technology
questions.explanation: The passage opens with the principle that pressure comes from elevation and then works out what follows from it for pump sizing, fire reserve and shape.
distractorNotes: no belief is set up and knocked down in the passage
the comparison of shapes appears only at the end, not throughout
the passage is not organized by time at all

questions.stem: A tank 150 feet above the neighborhood delivers roughly what pressure at street level?
choices: 65 pounds per square inch
43 pounds per square inch
150 pounds per square inch
100 pounds per square inch
questions.explanation: The passage states that a tank standing 150 feet up delivers about 65 pounds per square inch at street level.
distractorNotes: uses the per-foot rate as though it were the total
reports the height in place of the pressure
rounds to a figure the passage does not give

questions.stem: Which best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Solar and battery resources have made grid frequency impossible to control.
North American grids run at sixty cycles per second because regulators chose that standard.
Grid frequency reflects the balance of generation and load, and is defended in layers.
Grid operators must identify which generator has failed before they can respond.
questions.explanation: The passage establishes frequency as a consequence of balance, describes the three layers of response, and then explains how inverter-based resources have had to imitate the first layer.
distractorNotes: overstates a difficulty the passage says engineers have addressed
contradicts the passage, which says the number is read rather than set
reverses an explicit statement in the passage

questions.stem: According to the passage, frequency rises when
choices: generation exceeds demand
demand exceeds generation
operators increase the frequency setting
inertia is added to the system
questions.explanation: The passage states that when generation exceeds demand the spinning machines speed up and frequency rises.
distractorNotes: reverses the stated relationship
assumes a setting the passage denies exists
attributes the rise to a stabilizing factor rather than an imbalance

questions.stem: Which layer of response is described as acting first?
choices: Governor response
Inertia from rotating mass
Automatic generation control
Inverter injection
questions.explanation: The passage names inertia as the first layer and explicitly says it is not a decision at all.
distractorNotes: acts within seconds, after inertia
works over minutes and is described as third
is a later engineering addition, not the original first layer

questions.stem: As used in the passage, "donates" most nearly means
choices: contributes automatically, without being commanded
transfers on the condition that it be repaid
contributes only after a deliberate decision has been taken by an operator
wastes through unavoidable loss
questions.explanation: The sentence describes rotating mass resisting a speed change and supplying kinetic energy automatically, which the passage contrasts with a decision.
distractorNotes: reads a repayment condition into the word; restoring reserves later is a separate control action, not a condition attached to the inertial contribution
conflicts with the passage calling this layer not a decision at all
treats the energy as lost rather than usefully supplied to the grid

questions.stem: The passage implies that a grid with a very large share of inverter-based generation would
choices: require operators to abandon the sixty-cycle standard
be unable to detect a generator failure at all
drop in frequency faster after losing a generator unless inverters are programmed
have more inertia than a conventional grid
questions.explanation: The passage says such resources have no rotating mass, so the grid has less natural inertia and frequency falls faster, and that engineers program inverters to imitate the missing response.
distractorNotes: proposes a change the passage never suggests
contradicts the passage's account of frequency as an instant signal
reverses the passage's statement about rotating mass

questions.stem: The author says "the physics reports it" mainly to emphasize that frequency is
choices: identical at every point on every grid in the world
too complex for operators to influence
measured by instruments that can drift out of calibration
a measured result rather than a value anyone chooses
questions.explanation: The sentence closes a paragraph arguing that nobody sets the number and that it follows from the balance of generation and load.
distractorNotes: extends the claim beyond the interconnected grid discussed
overstates it; the passage describes deliberate responses
raises an accuracy issue the passage never mentions

questions.stem: Automatic generation control is described as working over
choices: milliseconds
minutes
seconds
hours
questions.explanation: The passage says the third layer works over minutes to return frequency exactly to sixty and restore reserves.
distractorNotes: belongs to the programmed inverter response
belongs to governor response
is longer than any interval the passage gives

questions.stem: The final sentence suggests that a programmed inverter response can be superior because it
choices: responds more slowly, which gives operators more time to think about it
can be adjusted, whereas a spinning mass cannot
eliminates the need for governor response entirely
produces more total energy than a turbine of the same size
questions.explanation: The passage closes by noting that a programmed response can be tuned while the physics of a spinning mass cannot.
distractorNotes: reverses the speed advantage the passage describes
claims a replacement the passage does not assert
compares energy output, which the passage does not discuss

questions.stem: The third paragraph is organized primarily by
choices: the cost of each response
the speed at which each response acts
the geographic location of each resource
the age of each technology
questions.explanation: The paragraph introduces the layers as distinguished by how quickly each acts and then moves from seconds to minutes.
distractorNotes: cost is not mentioned in the paragraph
location plays no part in that paragraph
the paragraph does not order the layers historically

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
choices: how standardizing cargo reshaped shipping, industry and ports
how engineers designed a stronger and lighter cargo box
why longshoremen resisted the introduction of new technology
how trade policy rather than technology drove industrial relocation
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the old loading process to standardization and then to effects on factory location, ports and the workforce.
distractorNotes: focuses on the steel, which the passage says was not the source of the gain
treats a consequence mentioned briefly as the central subject
picks one side of a debate the passage leaves open

questions.stem: Before containers, a ship might spend
choices: as long in port as it spent at sea
more time at sea than in port
a few hours in port between voyages
most of the year laid up awaiting repair
questions.explanation: The passage states that a ship might spend as long in port as it spent at sea.
distractorNotes: reverses the comparison given
understates the delay the passage describes
introduces a circumstance the passage never mentions

questions.stem: The statement that "the gain came not from the steel but from the agreement" most nearly means that
choices: steel prices were the main obstacle to adoption
the container was poorly built and needed frequent repair
labor agreements with dockworkers were the decisive factor
the value lay in common dimensions, not in the box itself
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the observation that one crane could lift them all and one chassis would fit any, which depends on shared dimensions.
distractorNotes: raises a cost issue the passage does not discuss
reads a quality complaint into a sentence about standardization
reads 'agreement' as a labor contract rather than a shared standard

questions.stem: According to the passage, cargo handling was expensive chiefly because it consumed
choices: more money than the voyage itself ever did
fuel and labor in roughly equal measure
labor and time in roughly equal measure
specialized equipment that wore out quickly
questions.explanation: The passage says it was expensive chiefly because it consumed labor and time in roughly equal measure.
distractorNotes: overstates a comparison the passage frames differently
substitutes fuel for time
names a cause the passage does not give

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a port with shallow water and little surrounding land would most likely have
choices: declined as the container system spread
specialized instead in handling containers for smaller coastal vessels
retained its workforce longer than deep-water ports
become a hub because it faced less competition
questions.explanation: The passage says ports that could not accommodate the cranes and land area declined quickly, sometimes within a decade.
distractorNotes: invents an adaptation the passage does not describe
conflicts with the account of rapid decline
reverses the outcome the passage reports

questions.stem: As used in the third paragraph, "loosened" most nearly means
choices: was deliberately relaxed by regulators
came apart entirely
grew more complicated
became less binding
questions.explanation: The sentence says the calculation that had tied factories to their customers loosened because the cost of distance fell, which is a weakening of a constraint.
distractorNotes: attributes the change to policy rather than falling costs
overstates it; the passage describes weakening, not elimination
substitutes complexity for reduced constraint

questions.stem: The author notes that economists still argue about attribution in order to
choices: show that the relocation of industry has been exaggerated
dismiss economists as unable to agree on anything
argue that trade policy mattered more than the container
acknowledge that the container's exact share is uncertain
questions.explanation: The passage reports that industries relocated and then notes the open question of how much to attribute to the container versus trade policy.
distractorNotes: denies a shift the passage treats as real
adopts a dismissive tone the passage does not take
takes a side the passage explicitly leaves open

questions.stem: The passage says the dock workforce
choices: stayed level but earned less
grew as ports expanded
contracted sharply
moved inland to work at new factories
questions.explanation: The passage states plainly that the workforce contracted sharply.
distractorNotes: describes a change in pay the passage does not report
contradicts the passage
invents a destination the passage never mentions

questions.stem: The final sentence implies that the container's effects were
choices: confined mostly to the shipping industry itself
smaller than historians originally believed
larger and less predictable than the efficiency case suggested
fully anticipated by the people who promoted it
questions.explanation: The sentence describes a change framed as a simple efficiency that redistributed work and wealth on a scale nobody had forecast.
distractorNotes: contradicts the passage's account of wider effects
reverses the sentence's emphasis
contradicts 'nobody had forecast'

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that
choices: modern fasteners have eliminated problems caused by expansion
thermal expansion is too small to matter in most buildings
aluminum should be avoided in structures exposed to weather
structures must accommodate thermal movement rather than resist it
questions.explanation: The passage argues that expansion will occur or else generate stress, and that good design directs the movement instead of preventing it.
distractorNotes: claims a solution the passage does not offer
contradicts the passage's central claim
draws a recommendation the passage never makes

questions.stem: A hundred-foot steel beam is said to grow about how much over a hundred-degree swing?
choices: A hundredth of an inch
Three quarters of a foot, measured along the beam
Three inches
Three quarters of an inch
questions.explanation: The passage gives roughly three quarters of an inch for that beam and that temperature change.
distractorNotes: understates the stated figure
misreads the unit, overstating the movement twelvefold
reports a figure the passage does not give

questions.stem: According to the passage, the stress in a restrained member is set mainly by
choices: the overall length of the restrained member
the stiffness of the material
the size of the movement that was prevented
the type of fastener used at the connection
questions.explanation: The passage states that the stress a restrained member generates is set by the stiffness of the material rather than by the size of the movement prevented.
distractorNotes: is ruled out; the passage separates stress from the size of the movement
is explicitly contrasted with the correct factor
belongs to the later discussion of joints

questions.stem: Compared with steel, aluminum is said to expand
choices: about ten times as much
about half as much for the same temperature change
about the same amount
about twice as much
questions.explanation: The passage says aluminum expands about twice as much as steel for the same temperature change.
distractorNotes: overstates the stated ratio
reverses the comparison
denies the difference the paragraph is built on

questions.stem: The passage implies that a rigid joint between aluminum and steel is likely to fail because
choices: the two materials move by different amounts, stressing the connection
aluminum is inherently weaker than steel
the joint is exposed to more weather than the members are
neither material is strong enough for the load applied
questions.explanation: The passage says such a joint concentrates stress at the fastener until something yields even though neither material alone would have been overstressed, and that the failure belongs to the connection.
distractorNotes: attributes failure to material strength, which the passage sets aside
invents an exposure difference the passage does not mention
contradicts the statement that neither alone would be overstressed

questions.stem: The author mentions bridge bearings, pipe loops and soft joints in masonry chiefly to
choices: argue that older construction methods were superior
show that bridges require more care than buildings
give varied examples of giving movement somewhere to go
explain how each of those components is manufactured
questions.explanation: The three examples follow the claim that designers provide somewhere for movement to go, and each illustrates directing movement rather than preventing it.
distractorNotes: introduces a judgment absent from the passage
draws a comparison the passage does not make
describes a purpose the passage does not pursue

questions.stem: As used in the final paragraph, "concessions" most nearly means
choices: rights granted to operate a business
formal agreements between contracting parties
allowances made to make up for a shortcoming
reductions in the price of materials
questions.explanation: The sentence denies that these features are concessions to sloppy work, meaning they are not allowances compensating for a deficiency.
distractorNotes: uses an unrelated commercial sense
uses a legal sense the sentence does not support
reads the word as a discount

questions.stem: The closing phrase about a structure finding "its own way to relieve the stress" suggests that
choices: structures gradually become more flexible as they age
unplanned movement leaves the structure to crack or deform
stress in a structure dissipates harmlessly over time
repairs will always restore a structure to its original condition
questions.explanation: The passage has already described buckling, cracking and fasteners yielding as what happens when movement is restrained, so an unplanned release is a failure.
distractorNotes: describes an adaptation the passage does not claim
contradicts the passage's warnings about buckling and cracking
addresses repair, which the passage does not discuss

questions.stem: Which best describes the structure of the passage?
choices: An effect, then its design consequences, then the worst case, then a conclusion
A problem is posed and two competing solutions are weighed
A historical development is traced from early practice to the present
A general rule is stated and then shown to have many exceptions
questions.explanation: The passage opens with expansion and restraint, moves to accommodations in design, then to dissimilar materials as the worst case, and ends with a general statement.
distractorNotes: no competing solutions are set against each other
the passage is not organized chronologically
the passage presents no exceptions to its rule
